nodes.label: Mandate established, Syria divided
nodes.full: Following the San Remo Conference's confirmation of the wartime Sykes-Picot arrangement and Faisal's defeat at Maysalun, France took formal control of Syria under a League of Nations Mandate and immediately divided it into several smaller statelets along regional and sectarian lines — the State of Damascus, the State of Aleppo, the Alawite State on the coast, and the Jabal Druze State — a deliberate administrative fragmentation many Syrian nationalists read as calculated to prevent the kind of unified Arab government France had just crushed at Maysalun.
nodes.src: Compare levant-1908-1920::c4 for the Battle of Maysalun this Mandate directly followed; League of Nations Mandate for Syria and Lebanon, formally confirmed 1922.

nodes.label: Greater Lebanon created
nodes.full: French High Commissioner General Gouraud proclaimed "Greater Lebanon," substantially expanding the old Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate's borders to incorporate Beirut, Tripoli, Sidon, Tyre and the Bekaa Valley — a considerably larger and more religiously mixed territory than the historically Christian-majority mountain it built on, establishing the basic territorial shape of the modern Lebanese state and, with it, the demographic balance later Lebanese confessional politics would have to manage.
nodes.src: Proclamation of Greater Lebanon (Grand Liban), 1 September 1920, at the Residence des Pins, Beirut.

nodes.label: Statelets built around religious community
nodes.full: France's initial division of Syria drew significantly on religious and sectarian geography — a distinct Alawite State on the coast, a Jabal Druze State in the south, Greater Lebanon's own carefully calculated religious balance — an administrative approach that both reflected genuine pre-existing communal distribution and simultaneously reinforced those same communal identities as primary units of formal governance, a legacy whose long-term political consequences for the region extended considerably beyond the Mandate period covered in this folio.
nodes.src: Comparative framing of French Mandate-era sectarian-territorial administrative divisions, 1920–1936; their longer-term political consequences are addressed in the later folios of this program covering independent Syria and Lebanon.

nodes.label: Trusteeship in name, colonial in practice
nodes.full: The League of Nations Mandate system formally obligated France to prepare Syria and Lebanon for eventual self-government as a "sacred trust of civilisation" rather than administer them as ordinary colonies — a legal distinction that made only a modest practical difference, since French officials retained ultimate decision-making authority, deployed military force against internal opposition, and only relinquished actual control when direct political pressure, not the Mandate's own supposedly built-in developmental timetable, eventually forced their hand.
nodes.src: League of Nations Mandate for Syria and Lebanon, Article 1's "sacred trust" language, confirmed 1922; the gap between this formal obligation and the Mandate's actual practice is a standard point of scholarly critique.

nodes.label: League of Nations fiction
nodes.full: The Mandate system emerged from the same postwar settlement that dissolved older-style formal empires as illegitimate, yet functioned in practice across Syria, Lebanon, Palestine and Iraq alike as a new international vocabulary for very similar continued great-power control — a genuinely novel legal category whose real-world operation, this folio's own narrative suggests, differed from direct colonialism considerably less than its "sacred trust" language implied.
nodes.src: Comparative framing of the interwar Mandate system (applied across Syria, Lebanon, Palestine and Iraq) as a new international-legal category whose practical operation closely resembled established colonial administration.

nodes.label: Roads, rail and ports for control
nodes.full: French Mandate authorities expanded roads, extended rail lines and improved port facilities at Beirut and elsewhere, infrastructure genuinely useful for civilian economic development but built and routed with equal attention to enabling rapid French military movement and administrative control across a territory prone to periodic unrest — development and control were never fully separable purposes in Mandate-era infrastructure planning.
nodes.src: Comparative assessment of French Mandate-era infrastructure investment's dual civilian-development and military-control purposes, 1920s–1940s.

nodes.label: Great Syrian Revolt and bombardment of Damascus
nodes.full: A major armed uprising against French rule began in the Jabal Druze region under Sultan al-Atrash's leadership and spread across much of Syria, drawing in nationalist fighters well beyond the Druze community itself — French forces responded with harsh measures including a sustained artillery bombardment of Damascus in October 1925 that killed substantial numbers of civilians and destroyed parts of the old city, a level of force that ultimately suppressed the revolt by 1927 but left it a lasting nationalist memory of French rule's coercive reality beneath its formal "trusteeship" language.
nodes.src: French bombardment of Damascus, October 1925, during the Great Syrian Revolt of 1925–1927.

nodes.label: Economic grievance feeds the revolt
nodes.full: Heavy new taxation, disrupted traditional trade patterns and the economic dislocation of the Mandate's administrative reorganisation compounded the Great Syrian Revolt's more explicitly political and nationalist grievances — rural communities in Jabal Druze and elsewhere experienced French rule's economic burden directly and immediately, in a way that made armed resistance a more urgent, material calculation than abstract nationalist ideology alone would have produced.
nodes.src: Comparative economic-historical framing of taxation and trade disruption as contributing material factors alongside nationalist ideology in the 1925–1927 Great Syrian Revolt.

nodes.label: Sultan al-Atrash
nodes.full: Sultan al-Atrash, a Druze leader from Jabal Druze with no particular ambition toward national leadership before French provocations pushed him into open revolt, found himself commanding a movement that drew fighters and sympathy from well beyond his own community — his later life as an honoured elder statesman of independent Syria, revered across sectarian lines, stands in notable contrast to the deliberately sect-based administrative categories French rule had tried to impose on the very same territory during his lifetime.
nodes.src: Sultan al-Atrash's leadership of the 1925–1927 Great Syrian Revolt; he remained a widely respected figure in independent Syria until his death in 1982.

nodes.label: Unified Syrian state re-emerges then stalls
nodes.full: France merged the Damascus and Aleppo statelets into a single Syrian State in 1924, a partial reversal of the initial fragmentation that nationalist pressure continued pushing further — culminating in a 1936 Franco-Syrian Treaty negotiated between French officials and the Syrian National Bloc that would have granted independence within a defined timeframe while preserving French strategic interests, an agreement the French parliament ultimately never ratified as the approach of a new European war reshaped French priorities.
nodes.src: Franco-Syrian Treaty of Independence, negotiated 1936, signed but never ratified by the French National Assembly before the Mandate's continuation into World War II.

nodes.label: Nationalist opposition persists
nodes.full: Syrian and Lebanese nationalist intellectuals and political organisers, working through the National Bloc and comparable movements, continued publishing, organising and negotiating throughout the Mandate period despite French press censorship and periodic exile or imprisonment of prominent figures — sustained political pressure that, alongside the more dramatic episodes of open revolt, steadily accumulated toward the eventual independence both territories achieved in the 1940s.
nodes.src: The National Bloc (al-Kutla al-Wataniya), the principal Syrian nationalist political organisation negotiating with and opposing French authorities throughout the Mandate period.

nodes.label: Vichy control and Free French invasion
nodes.full: Following France's 1940 defeat, the collaborationist Vichy government controlled Syria and Lebanon and permitted some German and Italian military use of local facilities, prompting a British and Free French invasion (Operation Exporter) in mid-1941 that ousted Vichy authorities — Free French General Catroux proclaimed both territories independent as the campaign concluded, a promise that would take several more years of political pressure to become practical reality.
nodes.src: Operation Exporter, June–July 1941; Catroux's independence proclamations, 1941, did not immediately translate into full practical French withdrawal.

nodes.label: Lebanon independence and National Pact
nodes.full: When Lebanon's government unilaterally amended the constitution to remove Mandate-era provisions in November 1943, French authorities arrested the president and prime minister — provoking a national uprising and, crucially, British pressure on wartime ally France to avoid alienating Arab opinion, forcing the officials' release and effective French acceptance of Lebanese independence, sealed by an unwritten "National Pact" between Christian and Muslim leaders establishing the confessional power-sharing arrangement — a Maronite president, a Sunni prime minister, a Shia speaker of parliament — that would structure Lebanese politics for generations afterward.
nodes.src: Lebanese independence crisis, November 1943; the unwritten National Pact agreement between President Bechara El Khoury and Prime Minister Riad al-Solh.

nodes.label: 1945 Levant Crisis
nodes.full: French forces bombarded Damascus a second time, including damage to the Syrian parliament building, in a final attempt to pressure the Syrian government into accepting continued French military privileges even after the war's end — an escalation that instead prompted direct British military intervention against their own wartime ally, forcing French forces to stand down and setting the immediate course toward complete withdrawal the following year.
nodes.src: May 1945 Levant Crisis; British Prime Minister Winston Churchill's government intervened directly against French forces, a rare instance of open Allied confrontation so soon after the war's European end.

nodes.label: Syria full independence
nodes.full: French troops completed their final withdrawal from Syria in April 1946 — an outcome forced not by negotiation but by the crisis covered in the Conflict entry below, in which Britain directly pressured wartime ally France to stand down militarily — ending the French Mandate outright and leaving Syria fully independent for the first time since Faisal's brief kingdom had been crushed twenty-six years earlier.
nodes.src: "Evacuation Day," 17 April 1946, commemorating the final French troop withdrawal from Syria, still marked annually as a Syrian national holiday.

nodes.label: Maysalun and the Sykes-Picot division enforced
nodes.full: Faisal’s defeat at Maysalun and the San Remo confirmation of Sykes-Picot hand Syria and Lebanon to France.
